heading: Headline
body: Utility infrastructure maintenance is a large market funded through regulated rates, and a well-trodden roll-up category with moderate margins. Crews and equipment are largely specific to each utility type, and margins change little with scale, which favors starting with one founder-owned gas distribution maintenance platform at about 6-8x EBITDA and adding units over time.

heading: The market
body:
Outsourced maintenance across gas, power and water is about $44-81B a year (est.), paid for through utility rates. Maintenance and replacement demand is supported by:
• investor-owned electric capex of ~$208B in 2025
• gas utility construction capex of $49.1B in 2023
• federally mandated gas inspection cycles
• 50-55% of distribution transformers older than 33 years
• water utilities renewing only ~0.8% of mains a year, a pace that would take ~125 years, while mains that break do so at ~53 years on average
• nuclear plants licensed to 80 years
Population growth (+0.5%) and headline load growth add less: they mostly fund new construction.

heading: The category
body: Maintenance roll-ups are a proven model. Shermco (~$1.6B to Blackstone), Pike (>$5B EV reported), USIC, Osmose and Azuria/Inframark were profitable sponsor exits. Multi-unit platforms have a weaker record: no one has built a scaled gas + power + water maintenance platform, the closest attempts failed (Williams, Orbital), and Artera, the largest gas roll-up, is highly leveraged. At least 26 sponsor-backed platforms compete for the same add-ons.

heading: Figures that should be revalidated
body:
• Scaled players: public data shows 15-20 companies with revenue around or above $1B, plus 26 sponsor-backed platforms, though fewer than 10 in each sub-segment.
• Shared crews and equipment: only ~15-27% of field headcount can move between power and gas or water (est.). Gas and water share more, at ~53%.
• Margins at scale: maintenance contracts earn about 8-10% EBITDA at most sizes. Scale mainly lifts the valuation multiple.
• Provider count: 18,877 utility-system construction firms (Census 2017), down from 25,227 in 2012. The maintenance-focused pool is much smaller.
• Asset age: NREL's transformer data, PHMSA's pipe inventory and the Utah State water main survey are stronger sources than grid-wide age estimates.

heading: A path the evidence favors
body:
• Start with one founder-owned gas distribution maintenance platform at ~6-8x EBITDA.
• Add water underground work in the same metros.
• Consider T&D later, as a separate operating company.
• Approach power generation, if at all, through testing or inspection add-ons.
A 9-11% margin and cash yield are a sounder underwriting basis than multiple expansion.

heading: A possible starting point
body: Natural gas distribution maintenance, built as an underground-utility platform that later adds water and wastewater work in the same metros

heading: Why
body:
Gas distribution maintenance is the only unit that combines four advantages:
1. Recurring work that is mandated on a calendar (49 CFR 192 leak surveys, cathodic protection, regulator inspections), plus replacement programs funded through state rate trackers.
2. A bounded target universe (~240 DCA members) that still includes founder-owned regional firms not held by sponsors.
3. The one sizable cross-unit synergy: gas shares crews and fleet with water underground work (~53% of movable headcount, ~65% of fleet value, est.).
4. The most direct links to Fulton's metals, fittings and freight businesses.

It also carries the clearest caution: Artera, the largest gas roll-up, is highly leveraged, and Centuri earns 8.3%. Buying small, at ~6-8x, with low leverage and no forced exit is the natural edge for permanent capital.

T&D is larger but heavily consolidated. Power generation is smaller and dominated by equipment makers' service arms.

heading: Step 1
body: Nov 2026: Consider focusing the first unit on gas distribution maintenance, with entry screens such as ~6-8x EBITDA; at least two utility MSA customers; most revenue from MSA or unit-rate maintenance rather than fixed-price or one-off low-bid work; a clean OSHA and EMR record; and leverage well below the levels that strained Artera.

heading: Step 2
body: Nov-Dec 2026: It may help to build a primary-source list of 40-60 founder- or family-owned gas contractors with $20-100M of revenue, drawing on the DCA directory (~240 members), state PUC filings on utility replacement programs (NJ, NY, MA, PA and MI hold the most remaining cast iron) and utility contractor prequalification lists.

heading: Step 3
body: Dec 2026: The independent gas regionals look like natural first conversations: Heath Consultants, R.H. White, Driver Pipeline and Larrett Energy, Banks Gas Services and Diversified Utility Services, and J.F. Kiely once family control is confirmed. Checking each one's size beforehand would save time. Danella would merit a safety review first, and sponsor auctions priced above the screen may be worth passing over.

heading: Step 4
body: Q1 2027: Diligence could focus on MSA terms and renewal dates, customer tenure, revenue mix by work type, PHMSA operator-qualification records, union status (UA/DCA vs non-union), and equipment ownership and fleet age. A reasonable milestone is one letter of intent by the end of Q1 2027 for a ~$50M-revenue platform (illustratively ~$5.5M EBITDA, ~$37-46M EV at 6.8-8.3x).

heading: Step 5
body: 2027: First add-ons could sit inside the platform's existing utility territories: leak survey, cathodic protection and regulator-station maintenance (all mandated under 49 CFR 192), plus hydro-excavation. These build density (est. 100-300 bps) and a larger share of each utility's spend.

heading: Step 6
body: 2027: A lean shared-services layer for safety, operator-qualification records, insurance and fleet purchasing would likely cost ~1-2% of revenue; a temporary margin dip around $150M of revenue is common.

heading: Step 7
body: 2027, after the D.C. Circuit rules on LCRI: Water underground work in the same metros is a natural second step, ideally taking lead service lines only under negotiated or unit-rate programs. Sewer cleaning and CCTV, and tank asset management (Carylon, Pittsburg Tank & Tower or Maguire, after ownership checks), are related options.

heading: Step 8
body: Nov 2026-2027: Links with Fulton's companies could start as small pilots: Imperial quoting buybacks of meter brass, service-line and cable scrap; Transend quoting pipe freight; Panther quoting fittings. Committing capex only against purchase orders keeps the downside small.

heading: Step 9
body: 2028 and later: T&D could be revisited as a separate operating company if a lower-middle-market distribution-maintenance or substation-testing firm becomes available within the screen. Power generation looks best approached through NETA testing or NDE add-ons.

heading: Step 10
body: Review points: a go or no-go on the target list in Jan 2027, a decision on the first platform in mid-2027, and a yearly re-underwriting against the watchlist and signals.

heading: Profile
body: A founder- or family-owned gas distribution maintenance contractor with about $50M of revenue and a 9-11% EBITDA margin (est.), working under MSAs with two to four gas utilities in one region. Typical work: main and service replacement, leak survey and repair, meter and regulator work, and cathodic protection.

heading: Who it would sell to
body: Gas distribution utilities (LDCs) under multi-year MSAs and unit-rate programs, about $30-40M a year (est.); transmission pipeline operators for integrity digs, $2-5M; and, in a second phase, water utilities in the same metros, $5-10M. The utilities recover this spending through state rate trackers paid by households and businesses.

heading: Who it would buy from
body: Field crews (pipelayers, operators, laborers, CDL drivers; UA/DCA or merit shop), about $16-20M a year in wages; paving, restoration and traffic-control subcontractors, $3-6M; insurance and surety, $1.5-2.5M; equipment rental, $1-2.5M; materials the utility does not furnish, from distributors such as Core & Main, $1-3M; vacuum excavators and drills from makers such as Vermeer; and hydro-excavation subcontractors such as Badger (all est.).

heading: Who it would compete with for work
body: Centuri, Artera (Miller Pipeline, Minnesota Limited) and Energy Services of America at scale; Quanta and MasTec units on larger programs; and regional independents in each territory. Utilities re-bid MSAs every three to five years, so safety record and unit prices decide renewals.

heading: Who it would compete with for deals
body: Sponsor-backed platforms buying gas and underground add-ons, including Sparus (Ridgemont), Delphi Infrastructure (MPE), USIC and Pro-Vac, plus public consolidators. Founder-owned firms sold off-market tend to price at ~6-8x EBITDA; auctions run higher.

heading: Add-on paths
body: Inside its territories: leak survey, cathodic protection, regulator-station maintenance and hydro-excavation. In the same metros: water main and service work, sewer cleaning and CCTV, and tank asset management.

heading: Imperial Group
body: Buys the platform's meter brass, steel service-line and cable scrap; small direct volumes (~$0.05-0.3M a year, est.). The larger opening is an introduction to the platform's utility customers, whose replacement programs generate $10-45M a year of gas scrap and $30-80M of lead and brass from water work (addressable market, est.).

heading: Transend Logistics
body: Moves pipe and materials from distributor yards to the platform's job sites (~$0.2-0.6M a year, est.), and could quote the pipe makers that supply the platform's utility customers.

heading: Panther Metalflow
body: Machined brass and steel fittings and meter-set components, sold through the platform's distributors or specified on its jobs (~$0.05-0.3M a year, est.). Most major materials are furnished by the utilities.

heading: AFCO Industries
body: Aluminum compartments and toolboxes for the platform's truck bodies, through upfitters (~$0.05-0.1M a year, est.).

heading: Stainless Foundry & Engineering
body: Occasional specialty castings for regulator-station and valve rebuilds; not sized.

heading: Metaltec
body: No clear link found.

heading: Overpaying in a sponsor-crowded market (Pike >$5B reported, Shermco ~$1.6B, public peers at ~15.2x)
body: Favoring founder- and family-owned firms at ~6-8x, passing on auctions priced above the screen, and building the pipeline from primary rosters rather than banker books.

heading: Thin margins that do not expand with scale (MSA work earns 8-10%; ~+0.3 pts net from $50M to $500M, est.)
body: Underwriting 9-11% steady-state margins and cash yield, giving little credit for cross-unit crew flex, and keeping shared costs to ~1-2% of revenue.

heading: Leverage meeting utility buying power, as at Artera (>$2.5B of debt) and Orbital
body: Permanent capital with modest leverage (Centuri deleveraged to 2.5x), staggered maturities, and a preference for several small deals over one large one.

heading: Creep into fixed-price and low-bid work (Williams; margin swings at MYR and MasTec Pipeline)
body: Capping fixed-price and low-bid revenue in the platform criteria, favoring add-ons whose work is MSA or unit-rate, and reporting job-level margins from day one.

heading: Customer concentration and loss of an MSA (Williams lost large contracts in 2022)
body: At least two utility MSAs at entry, diligence on renewal dates and tenure, and growth with existing customers before new geographies.

heading: Finite replacement programs: cast iron is ~16K miles, ~11-16 years from done
body: Leaning toward bare steel, vintage plastic, service lines and mandated compliance work, which run into the 2040s.

heading: Regulatory and funding timing: PHMSA leak rule withdrawn, LCRI in litigation, IIJA SRF money ended in FY2026
body: A base case built on existing state rate-tracker programs, with federal rules and federal money treated as upside.

heading: Safety and qualification exposure (OSHA trench cases; gas operator qualifications specific to each utility)
body: Screening OSHA history and EMR, and centralizing operator-qualification records and the safety program. Repeat trench citations are a reason to pass.

heading: Labor scarcity and split union jurisdictions (UA/DCA, IBEW, LIUNA)
body: Mapping union status for each target, not assuming crews can move between units or regions, and budgeting ~0.7 pts for wage harmonization.

heading: Affordability pressure on utility rates and O&M budgets
body: Favoring replacement programs that utilities capitalize and earn a return on over O&M work they expense.

heading: Centuri's base gross margin and adj. EBITDA against its $280-310M 2026 guide
body: The best public read on gas and electric MSA economics. A miss signals utility pricing pressure.

heading: PHMSA leak detection and repair rule published in the Federal Register
body: A federal driver for leak survey and repair returns, which raises the value of compliance-service add-ons.

heading: D.C. Circuit decision on LCRI (AWWA v. EPA)
body: If the rule is upheld, lead-line work and Imperial's lead and brass flows proceed toward the Nov 2027 deadline. If it is narrowed, the water entry slips.

heading: FY2027 State Revolving Fund appropriations
body: Shows how deep the water funding cliff is now that IIJA supplemental money has ended.

heading: State PUC approvals of gas replacement riders in NJ, NY, MA, PA and MI
body: Shows whether gas replacement work will last where most cast iron remains.

heading: Prices paid in sponsor exits of lower-middle-market utility services (e.g. Sparus, held since 2021; the reported USG Water Solutions sale)
body: Shows whether ~6-8x entry is still realistic. Above ~9-10x, shift to smaller add-ons or slow down.

heading: Artera refinancing, rating actions or asset sales
body: Gas assets could come loose as carve-out platforms. Deeper distress is a warning about MSA economics.

heading: EEI's actual capex against its ~$207.9B 2025 projection
body: Confirms the size of the T&D pool; EEI says first-year projections tend to run high.

heading: Nuclear license renewals and restarts (Nine Mile Point 1, Palisades, Crane)
body: Sets the size and timing of the outage and inspection niche for NDE and testing add-ons.

heading: EIA commercial load data and Grid Strategies' next load forecast
body: Shows whether data-center growth holds. This is mainly a construction signal and second-order for maintenance.

heading: Caveats
body:
Many central figures are analyst estimates, not reported data:
• the market size by unit ($44-81B)
• the labor and fleet overlap matrices
• synergy basis points
• the illustrative P&L and margin bridge
• the flows shown for the prospective platform on the market map
• the size of the platform-quality universe
• the pre-tax cash yield

Items that are unverified or weakly sourced:
• The 1921 build date of PG&E's Caribou-Palermo line (press reporting on PG&E records).
• MIT's 8,000 mi/yr transmission build rate (excluded) and the ~90% replacement share of transmission spend.
• Artera's current rating (a Dec 2025 S&P action was not confirmed).
• Pike's >$5B value (press-reported).
• Asplundh's revenue and Day & Zimmermann's current revenue.
• The current owners of USG Water Solutions, Carylon, Pittsburg Tank & Tower and Maguire Iron.
• The PJM +41% wholesale price figure.

Six-digit NAICS firm counts conflict across aggregators and were not used. The share of gas mains over 50 years old rests on 2021 PHMSA data and should be re-pulled.

The candidate list over-represents sponsor-owned and web-visible firms. Founder-owned $10-50M businesses need primary rosters (DCA, NETA, NASSCO, AWWA, state PUC lists). Lower-middle-market multiples are all-industry (GF Data), not utility-specific.

Not researched here: state gas-transition policy and long-run gas demand.

Out of scope: sponsor economics and any specific live deal process.
